passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text:
ANNUAL

Annual data on quantities for crude oil, petroleum products, natural gas and manufactured gases, electricity and derived heat, solid fossil fuels, renewables and wastes, and hydrogen covering the full spectrum of the energy sector from supply through transformation to final consumption by sector and fuel type.

Also, annual imports and exports data of various energy carriers by country of origin and destination, as well as infrastructure information.

Data on annual statistics are collected via standard questionnaires according to Annex B of the Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 October 2008 on energy statistics

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text:
DISAGGREGATED FINAL ENERGY CONSUMPTION

Annual data on quantities for the same fuels as the standard annual data, covering and disaggregating further final energy consumption by sector and fuel type. The inflowing data are delivered by reporting countries to Eurostat via four specific questionnaires, focusing on final energy consumption in:

- The Households/Residential sector

- The Industry sector

- The Services sector

- Transport activities (in any sector)

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text:
Data on disaggregated final energy consumption statistics are collected via standard questionnaires according to Annex B of the Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 October 2008 on energy statistics

In disaggregated final energy consumption statistics, an aggregate represents an entire family of fuels and not just the fuels displayed in the tables. As an example, in nrg_d_serq_n, the Oil and petroleum products aggregate does not only represent LPG and Gas/diesel oil, but also all other fuels present in the family of Oil and petroleum products (such as Fuel oil, Motor gasoline, etc.).



MONTHLY

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text:
The monthly energy data collections cover the most important energy commodities:

- Crude oil & Petroleum products

- Natural gas

- Solid fuels

- Electricity

For each of the above mentioned commodities the inflowing data are delivered by the reporting countries to Eurostat via separate dedicated questionnaires.

Data on monthly statistics are collected via standard questionnaires according to Annex C of the Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 October 2008 on energy statistics



SHORT-TERM MONTHLY

The short-term monthly energy data collection covers the imports and supply of crude oil.

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text: Data on monthly short term statistics are collected via standard questionnaires according to Annex D of the Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 October 2008 on energy statistics.

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text:
Energy statistics is an integral part of the European system of statistics. Therefore, they also rely on classifications and nomenclatures developed in other fields.

The classification of the economic activities both in carrying out the surveys and in presenting the results is in accordance to NACE Rev.2 .

Classification of energy products (commodities/carriers) is in general highly consistent with the UN’s International Recommendations for Energy Statistics (especially its chapter 3: “Standard International Energy Product Classification”).

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text:
Energy statistics data covers all major sectors of the economy that are involved in the production, trade, energy transformation or energy consumption (e.g. energy sector, industrial sector, transport, commercial and public services, agricultural/forestry/fishing and households, for annual data).

For further detail information on divisions, groups or class please consult the annual reporting instructions or monthly reporting instructions .

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text: For energy statistics, definitions, concepts and methodology are harmonised at international level. The methodology is described in the Energy Statistics Manual . Definitions of Annex A of  Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008 on energy statistics apply.

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text:
The statistical unit may vary in energy statistics. A statistical unit in energy statistics can be for example: enterprises, local units, establishment or household.

Reporting units in energy statistics might be: producers, importers, exporters of oil and petroleum products, households.

For detailed information on statistical units, see Council Regulation (EEC) No 696/93 of 15 March 1993 on the statistical units for the observation and analysis of the production system in the Community (Official Journal of the European Communities No L 076, 30 March 1993, p. 1) , Section III of 15 March 1993 on the statistical units for the observation and analysis of the production system in the Community.

passages.text: Not available - not produced by Eurostat. Specific national information can be found in the national metadata files built on the basis of the national quality reports .

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text:
Annual data are available from 1990 onwards for the vast majority of countries, monthly data from 2008 onwards and short-term monhtly data on crude oil imports and supply from 2005 onwards.

Disaggregated final energy consumption data are available for the vast majority of countries from 2015 onwards for households, from 2020 onwards for industry and from 2022 for services and transport activities onwards.

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text: The concept of base period is not applicable for energy statistics as there is no “index number” or a “constant series”.

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text:
Energy quantities statistics are collected and published by Eurostat in order to:

- Provide the Commission with harmonised, reliable and relevant statistical information needed to define, implement, monitor and evaluate Commission policies in the energy sector.

- Provide the EU institutions, national administrations, enterprises, professional associations and EU citizens with high quality statistical services and products in the field of energy.

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text:
Eurostat conducts two types of evaluations that assess Eurostat's performance in general:

- Evaluations of the Community Statistical Programmes

- User Satisfaction Surveys

Please see  more details on the Eurostat website .

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text: Data on energy is submitted on the basis of energy questionnaires employing an standardised methodology. Eurostat receives disaggregated data which are used to countercheck the results and to ensure consistency with the total amount of energy consumption. The accuracy of the basic data depends on the quality of the national statistical systems and may vary from country to country. Eurostat checks each data collection against analogue elements in other data collections (e.g. monthly against annual, disaggregated final energy consumption against annual).

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text: In several countries and for most energy commodities data provision by the companies is required by law. However, emerging liberalisation process in some countries may to some extent negatively affect accuracy in some cases. From time to time detailed surveys targeted to single sub-items (e.g. Wood consumption in households) are carried out to improve the methodology.

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text: Energy domain provides highly comparable annual energy statistics. Eurostat verifies, to the extent possible, if the reported data respect the prescribed methodology. The underlying data collection methods are however the responsibility of the reporting countries. The methodology for reporting energy statistics is harmonised for all European countries (EU Member States, EFTA countries, EU Candidate Countries, Energy Community Contracting Parties) and also with the OECD energy statistics. In general, the energy statistics compiled by Eurostat is coherent with the International Recommendations for Energy Statistics adopted by the United Nations Statistical Commission in 2011.

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text:
Comparability over time is ensured with a solid methodology harmonised on international level that is stable over long periods. Occasional breaks in time series are present due to the developments of statistical systems on national level and the level of detailed information (micro data) available at national level.

In general comparability is very high in the last 15 years and somewhat lower for older periods. In addition, introduction of new statistical information in the most recent data collections can lead to breaks in series until information is compiled and provided by reporting countries.

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text: Data are checked in detail for internal consistency/coherence in full cooperation with the countries concerned. Details checks involve the consistency of time series, detection of outliers, efficiency of energy transformation processes and also checks on utilization factors.

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text:
Data are obtained from the National Administrations competent for energy statistics. Depending on the reporting country and the specific monthly process, the data providers can be:

- National Statistical Institutes

- Ministries

- Energy Agencies

- Professional Associations

Questionnaires in standardized electronic format are collected from the national authorities via data transmission over the Internet. Data files have to be transmitted by the Member States to Eurostat via the Single Entry Point (SEP) following the implementing procedures of eDAMIS (electronic Data files Administration and Management Information System).

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text: More information can be found in the national metadata files build on the basis of the national quality reports.

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text:
Countries report to Eurostat basic data in the relevant units as defined in Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008 on energy statistics . Country aggregations, such as European Union or Euro Area are formed by the aggregation of data from individual countries.

In energy statistics, aggregations are formed by the sum of publicly available data, except in the following datasets where aggregations are formed by the sum of all data (public and confidential):

- Imports and supply of crude oil (COIR_M – short-term monthly)

- Final energy consumption in industry (ESIND_A – disaggregated annual)

- Final energy consumption in services (ESSER_A – disaggregated annual)

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text: In the datasets mentioned above, a (n,k) rule is applied for the treatment of confidential data with the (3,80) parameters. If there are 3 or more confidential values in the aggregate, and the sum of any two of these confidential values is not larger than 80% of the total confidential values, the aggregate is published.

passages.title: Energy statistics - quantities (nrg_quant)
passages.text: No adjustments of data are performed in a systematic way, because energy statistics are collected according to internationally harmonised methodology and standards.

passages.title: Primary energy consumption (sdg_07_10)
passages.text:
The indicator measures the total energy needs of a country excluding all non-energy use of energy carriers (e.g. natural gas used not for combustion but for producing chemicals).

"Primary Energy Consumption" covers the energy consumption by end users such as industry, transport, households, services and agriculture, plus energy consumption of the energy sector itself for production and transformation of energies, losses occurring during the transformation of energies (e.g. the efficiency of electricity production from combustible fuels) and the transmission and distribution losses of energy.

passages.title: Energy intensity (nrg_ind_ei)
passages.text:
Energy intensity is calculated as units of energy per unit of GDP. Indicator expressed in chain linked volumes is more suitable to be used to compare different time periods in one country, while PPS values are more suitable to be used to compare across countries in one specific year.

Energy data are from Eurostat's dataset nrg_bal_s and GDP data are from Eurostat's dataset nama_10_gdp .

nrg_bal_s:

- SIEC: TOTAL

- NRG_BAL: GAE

- UNIT: KTOE

nama_10_gdp:

- NA_ITEM: B1GQ

- UNIT: CLV05_MEUR, CLV10_MEUR, CLV15_MEUR, CP_MPPS_EU27_2020

Calculation examples:

passages.title: Energy intensity (nrg_ind_ei)
passages.text:
Energy per GDP = 1000 * KTOE / CLV10_MEUR (Chain linked volumes, index 2010=100)
Energy per GDPPPS = 1000* KTOE / CP_MPPS (Current prices, million purchasing power standards)

Resulting calculations are rounded to 2 decimal places.

passages.title: Energy intensity (nrg_ind_ei)
passages.text:
KGOE_TEUR_PPS: Kilograms of oil equivalent (KGOE) per thousand euro in purchasing power standards (PPS)

- EI_GDP_PPS: Energy intensity of GDP in purchasing power standards (PPS)

KGOE_TEUR: Kilograms of oil equivalent (KGOE) per thousand euro

- EI_GDP_CLV05: Energy intensity of GDP in chain linked volumes (2005)

- EI_GDP_CLV10: Energy intensity of GDP in chain linked volumes (2010)

- EI_GDP_CLV15: Energy intensity of GDP in chain linked volumes (2015)

passages.title: Energy productivity (sdg_07_30)
passages.text: The indicator measures the amount of economic output that is produced per unit of gross available energy. The gross available energy represents the quantity of energy products necessary to satisfy all demand of entities in the geographical area under consideration. The economic output is either given as in the unit of Euros in chain-linked volumes to the reference year 2010 at 2010 exchange rates or in the unit PPS (Purchasing Power Standard). The former is used to observe the evolution over time for a specific region while the latter allows comparing Member States in a given year.

passages.title: Energy imports dependency (nrg_ind_id)
passages.text:
Energy imports dependency  shows the share of total energy needs of a country met by imports from other countries. The  rate shows the proportion of energy that an economy must import. It is defined as net energy imports divided by gross available energy, expressed as a percentage. It can be defined for all products total as well as for individual fuels (for example: crude oil, natural gas). All data are from energy balances.

Energy dependence = (imports – exports) / gross available energy

A negative dependency rate indicates a net exporter of energy while a dependency rate in excess of 100 % indicates that energy products have been stocked.

passages.title: Energy imports dependency (nrg_ind_id)
passages.text:
By definition, all nuclear energy production counts as domestic production, regardless the origin of fuel for nuclear fission/fussion. In similar manner, all renewables and biofules count as domestic production, regardless the origin of feedstock (biomass or waste) from which it was produced.

Individual national data includes intra-EU trade. For EU aggregates, the net imports in principle cancel out all intra-EU trade (abstracting from statistical discrepancies in reported trade data: imports reported by country A from country B are not always exactly the same as exports by country B to country A).

passages.title: Import dependency on third countries by fuel type (nrg_ind_id3cf)
passages.text:
The calculation formula for this indicator is the following:

where:

TIMP represents import in units as reported in trade tables of energy questionnaires

BIMP represents imports in energy balances

PP represents primary production

RR  represents recovered and recycled products

SC  represents stock changes

C represents country

C∈EU   for each country C of the EU

F  represents individual elements of a fuel group (i.e. one fuel type)

F∈FG for each fuel F in fuel group FG

FG represents Fuel Groups, which are listed below (presented as dimension SIEC in the database):

passages.title: Import dependency on third countries by fuel type (nrg_ind_id3cf)
passages.text:
[TOTAL] Total [Overall]  is a category covering the total of the following categories [CF_R] Combustible fuels - renewable, [C0000X0350-0370] Solid fossil fuels, [SFF_OTH] Other solid fossil fuels, [G3000] Natural gas, [O4000XBIO] Oil and petroleum products (excluding biofuel portion) and [E7000] Electricity.

[CF_R] Combustible fuels - renewable  [Combustible renewables (biofuels)] includes Primary solid biofuels, Charcoal, Pure biogasoline, Blended biogasoline, Pure biodiesels, Blended biodiesels, Pure bio jet kerosene, Blended bio jet kerosene, Other liquid biofuels and Biogases.

[SFF_OTH] Other solid fossil fuels [Other fossil fuels and wastes] includes Peat, Peat products, Oil shale and oil sands, Industrial waste (non-renewable), Renewable municipal waste, Non-renewable municipal waste.

[E7000] Electricity [Electricity and heat (including nuclear) ] includes Hydro, Geothermal, Wind, Solar thermal, Solar photovoltaic, Tide, wave, ocean, Ambient heat (heat pumps), Nuclear heat, Electricity and Heat.

Methodological drawbacks of this indicator:

- When countries cannot identify the correct origin of imports and report “non specified”, the accuracy of data is lowered. In addition, confidentiality issues create distortions in data, especially when data are supressed and included in “non specified”.

passages.title: Import dependency on third countries by fuel type (nrg_ind_id3cf)
passages.text: - Reporting methodology for liquefied natural gas (LNG) results in attributing the re-exported LNG to the country with regasification terminal. In a similar manner, petroleum products refined from imported crude oil that are exported are not considered as those from 3rd countries. Thus import dependency is “reallocated” from the final consumption country to the country with LNG terminal or that with oil refinery.

passages.title: Import dependency on third countries by fuel type (nrg_ind_id3cf)
passages.text: - For oil and coal, imports by origin are available only in tonnes. This creates problems when combining products in the indicator. The implemented solution is to apply, at the level of each individual fuel, the ratio calculated from trade figures, to the overall imports in energy balances. This means that we keep distinctions between fuels and we keep only the distortion caused by import origins and export destinations. For example: we do not mix imports of crude oil with motor gasoline, but we are not be able to distinguish between light and heavy crude oils.

passages.title: Import dependency on third countries by fuel type (nrg_ind_id3cf)
passages.text: - In energy statistics, there is no trade for feedstock for biofuel production (e.g. animal fats, vegetable oils) and nuclear fuel (e.g. uranium, plutonium). All biofuels and nuclear energy is counted as primary domestic production, regardless of the origin of material used for its actual production. This is the historical convention for import dependency indicators.

passages.title: Import dependency on third countries by fuel type (nrg_ind_id3cf)
passages.text: - There is no trade reported for some fuels in energy statistics. The imports of the following fuels are not included in the data collected by Eurostat and are thus not part of the indicator for import dependency: primary solid biofuels, charcoal, biogas, industrial wastes, renewable and non-renewable municipal wastes, gas coke, oil shale and oil sands.

passages.title: Import dependency on third countries by fuel type (nrg_ind_id3cf)
passages.text: - Electricity and heat produced from combustible fuels are presented as import dependency of these combustible fuels. In other words, we count import dependency of a natural gas power plant as import dependency of natural gas and not as import dependency of electricity. Therefore the denominator of fuel group “electricity and heat” excludes combustible fuels. In addition, it is important to note that electricity transits via Switzerland count as exchanges with 3rd countries (e.g. flows between France and Italy).

passages.title: Energy import origin concentration index by fuel (nrg_ind_ioc)
passages.text:
This indicator is calculated across every fuel, for which import origins are reported in the annual energy statistics, which are the source data for this calculation.

I = Imports

CV = calorific value

FG = fuel group (i.e. oil, coal renewables, ...)

F = individual fuel (i.e. crude oil, natural gas, biogas, electricity, ...)

Resulting calculations are rounded to 4 decimal places.

passages.title: Energy import origin concentration index by fuel (nrg_ind_ioc)
passages.text: It needs to be recognised that we are making calculations over products reported in tonnes and in reality we are grouping products with significantly different calorific values. This is partly mitigated by using product-specific calorific values, however there are no origin-specific calorific values. In practice the calculation is done by applying the portion calculated in tonnes to the total imports in the energy balance.

passages.title: Energy self-reliance (nrg_ind_esr)
passages.text:
Energy self-reliance is calculated using the following ratio:

- numerator: primary production + recovered & recycled products

- denominator: primary production + recovered & recycled products + imports + stock draw

Resulting calculations are expressed as percentage and rounded to 2 decimal places.

Energy data are from Eurostat's dataset nrg_bal_s.

While this indicator could be in principle calculated for any fuel group, it is the most meaningful for the “Total of all fuels” which is shown in the database.

passages.title: Electricity production capacities by main fuel groups and operator (nrg_inf_epc)
passages.text:
These are data collected via the annual electricity and heat questionnaire and the annual renewables questionnaire, according to Annex B of the  Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008  of the European Parliament and of the Council of 22 October 2008 on energy statistics. The variables are:

- Total capacity (MWe)

- Capacity by source of electricity production (MWe)

- Capacity by type of generation in power plants using combustible fuels (MWe)

- Capacity by type of firing and by type of fuel used in power plants using combustible fuels (MWe)

passages.title: Electricity production capacities by main fuel groups and operator (nrg_inf_epc)
passages.text:
All reported capacities are broken down by type of supplier (main activity producer or auto-producer) in nrg_inf_epc. For plants based on combustion of fuels the capacity is further divided by type of technology of the generating plant (steam, internal combustion….) in nrg_inf_epct, by type of firing and by type of fuels.  The dataset  nrg_inf_epcrw offers more detailed renewable fuels.

Total capacity calculated from the aggregation of individual categories coming from each of the datasets could yield slightly different values. indeed, the data come from different sources (different questionnaires) and different use of decimal places and rounding could result in these differences.

passages.title: Electricity production capacities by main fuel groups and operator (nrg_inf_epc)
passages.text: A particular case is solar photovoltaic (PV) energy. Two types of capacities are displayed: AC and DC. A solar PV system works by capturing sunlight using photovoltaic cells and converting it into DC (direct current) electricity. The DC electricity is then usually converted into AC (alternate current) electricity using an inverter, as most electrical devices and systems use AC power. Therefore, there are differences between the solar PV capacity in DC and in AC. The former is the electrical capacity of the installed panel(s) that generate(s) electricity in DC. e. the maximum AC power the inverter(s) can provide.

passages.title: Electricity production capacities by main fuel groups and operator (nrg_inf_epc)
passages.text: For calculating the solar PV capacity that contributes to the total electrical capacity of the country, the smallest of the two (AC and DC) is taken into account. If only one of the two is available, then it is that one that contributes to the total electrical capacity of the country.

passages.title: Electricity production capacities by main fuel groups and operator (nrg_inf_epc)
passages.text:
Comparability over time is ensured with a solid methodology harmonised on international level that is stable over long periods. Occasional breaks in time series are present due to the developments of statistical systems on national level and the level of detailed information (micro data) available at national level.

In general comparability is very high in last 10 years and for older periods slowly decreasing. In addition, introduction of new statistical information in the most recent data collections can lead to breaks in series until information is compiled and provided by reporting countries.

passages.title: Heat pumps - technical characteristics by technologies (nrg_inf_hptc)
passages.text:
Data on technical characteristics of heat pumps cover the Net maximum thermal capacity, the Average Seasonal Performance Factor (SPF) and the Average time usage.

1. Net maximum thermal capacity - classification by technology. The net maximum capacity is the maximum active thermal energy that can be supplied, continuously, with all plant running. The reported figures should relate to the maximum capacities on 31st of December and be expressed in megawatts (MWth) and all heat pumps should be included. If, for some reason, only gross capacity data can be provided, please state this clearly.

passages.title: Heat pumps - technical characteristics by technologies (nrg_inf_hptc)
passages.text:
2. Average Seasonal Performance Factor (SPF). The SPF is weighted average seasonal performance factor, which refers to the ‘net seasonal coefficient of performance in active mode’ (SCOPnet) for electricity driven heat pumps or ‘net seasonal primary energy ratio in active mode’ (SPERnet) for thermally driven heat pumps.

3. Average time usage. The Average time usage means the assumed annual number of hours a heat pump has to provide heat to deliver the total usable heat delivered by heat pumps. The figure should be reported in the unit of hour (hr).

passages.title: Nuclear energy facilities (nrg_inf_nuc)
passages.text:
These are statistics concerning the civil use of nuclear energy. The variables are:

- enrichment capacity,

- production capacity of fresh fuel elements,

- production capacity of MOX fuel fabrication plants,

- production of fresh fuel elements,

- production of MOX fuel elements,

- production of nuclear heat,

- annual average burnup of definitively discharged irradiated fuel elements,

- production of Uranium and Plutonium in reprocessing plants and

- production capacity of Uranium and Plutonium of reprocessing plants.

passages.title: Nuclear energy facilities (nrg_inf_nuc)
passages.text:
Data collection covers in principle Member States of the European Union, Iceland and Norway. However, only 13 EU Member States (Belgium, Bulgaria, Czech Republic, Germany, Spain, France, Hungary, The Netherlands, Romania, Slovenia, Slovakia, Finland, and Sweden) operate nuclear reactors. Data for UK is available until 2019.

EU aggregate is shown for all variables, except for annual average burnout of definitely disharged irradiated elements.

passages.title: Nuclear energy facilities (nrg_inf_nuc)
passages.text: Energy statistics is an integral part of the European system of statistics. Therefore, they also rely on classifications and nomenclatures developed in other fields.

passages.title: Nuclear energy facilities (nrg_inf_nuc)
passages.text:
The definitions of the variables used in this database are the following:

1. Enrichment capacity.  It refers to the annual separative work capacity of operational enrichment plants, which separate or concentrate the Uranium-235 isotope, from 0.7 % to 3-5 %. This operation is necessary in order to obtain suitable nuclear fuel.

2. Production of fresh fuel elements in nuclear fuel fabrication plants . It refers to the step following enrichment in the nuclear fuel cycle, in other words, the process in which the nuclear fuel is manufactured in order to be utilized in nuclear power reactors. Rods or other partial products are not included. Fabrication plants producing MOX fuel are also excluded.

passages.title: Nuclear energy facilities (nrg_inf_nuc)
passages.text:
3. Production capacity of fresh fuel elements. It refers to the annual production capacity of fuel fabrication plants. MOX fuel fabrication plants are excluded.

4. Production of MOX fuel elements. It refers to the production of finished fresh Mixed Oxide (mixture of Plutonium and Uranium) fuel elements in MOX fuel fabrication plants. Rods or other partial products are not included.

5. Production capacity of MOX fuel fabrication plants. It refers to the annual production capacity of MOX fuel fabrication plants.

passages.title: Nuclear energy facilities (nrg_inf_nuc)
passages.text: 6. Production of nuclear heat. It refers to the total amount of heat generated by nuclear reactors (heat content of the steam leaving the reactor) for the production of electricity or for other useful applications of heat (there are a few cases where some steam is taken from reactors and used for district heating purposes as well as electricity generation).

passages.title: Nuclear energy facilities (nrg_inf_nuc)
passages.text: 7. Annual average burnup of definitively discharged irradiated fuel elements. Burnup refers to the extent to which nuclear fuel is consumed in a reactor and is a measure of how much energy is extracted from a primary nuclear fuel source. The annual average burnup refers to the calculated average of the burnup of the fuel elements which have been definitively discharged from the nuclear reactors during the concerned reference year. Excludes fuel elements that are temporarily discharged and are likely to be reloaded again later.

passages.title: Nuclear energy facilities (nrg_inf_nuc)
passages.text:
8. Production of Uranium and Plutonium in reprocessing plants. Reprocessing consists of recovering fissile and fertile materials from used nuclear fuel in order to provide fresh fuel for existing and future nuclear power plants. The process of reprocessing used nuclear fuel allows the recovery of unused uranium and plutonium from the original fuel and reduces the volume of material to be disposed of as high-level waste.

9. Capacity (Uranium and Plutonium) of reprocessing plants. It refers to the annual reprocessing capacity of Uranium and Plutonium.

passages.title: Gas prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_202)
passages.text: European statistics on natural gas prices for household and final non-household customers.

passages.title: Gas prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_202)
passages.text: Internal Eurostat classification system based on annual natural gas consumption bands and tax levels.

passages.title: Gas prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_202)
passages.text: Household sector and final non-household sector (industry, services, offices, agriculture, etc).

passages.title: Gas prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_202)
passages.text:
The prices are collected in national currencies per GJ and according to different bands of consumption.

For the households sector, these bands are:

- D1: Customers consuming less than 20 GJ.

- D2: Customers consuming 20 GJ or more but less than 200 GJ.

- D3: Customers consuming 200 GJ or more.

For the final non-households sector, the bands are:

- I1: Customers consuming less than 1000 GJ.

- I2: Customers consuming 1000 GJ or more but less than 10000 GJ.

- I3: Customers consuming 10000 GJ or more but less than 100000 GJ.

- I4: Customers consuming 100000 GJ or more but less than 1000000 GJ.

- I5: Customers consuming 1000000 GJ or more but less than 4000000 GJ.

passages.title: Gas prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_202)
passages.text:
- I6: Customers consuming 4000000 GJ or more.

There exist 2 different levels of disagregation for semestrial and annual prices:

1- Semestrial prices:

These prices are reported twice a year and are divided in 3 levels:

- Level 1 prices: Prices excluding taxes and levies.

- Level 2 prices: Prices excluding VAT and other recoverable taxes and levies.

- Level 3 prices: Prices including all taxes and levies.

2- Annual prices:

These prices are reported once a year together with the data for the second semester and are divided into the following components and taxes:

passages.title: Gas prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_202)
passages.text:
- Energy and supply: commodity price for natural gas paid by the supplier or the price of natural gas at the point of entry into the transmission system, including, if applicable, the following end-user costs: storage costs plus costs relating to the sale of natural gas to final customers.

- Network cost: transmission and distribution tariffs, transmission and distribution losses, network costs, after-sale service costs, system service costs and meter rental and metering costs.

- Value added taxes (VAT): as defined in Council Directive 2006/112/EC.

- Renewable taxes: taxes, fees, levies or charges relating to the promotion of renewable energy sources, energy efficiency and CHP generation.

passages.title: Gas prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_202)
passages.text:
- Capacity taxes: taxes, fees, levies or charges relating to strategic stockpiles, capacity payments and energy security; taxes on natural gas distribution; stranded costs and levies on financing energy regulatory authorities or market and system operators.

- Environmental taxes: taxes, fees, levies or charges relating to air quality and for other environmental purposes; taxes on emissions of CO 2  or other greenhouse gases. This component includes the excise duties.

passages.title: Gas prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_202)
passages.text:
- All other taxes: taxes, fees, levies or charges not covered by any of the previous four categories: support for district heating; local or regional fiscal charges; island compensation; concession fees relating to licences and fees for the occupation of land and public or private property by networks or other devices.

In addition to these elements, the network cost is split into the respective shares of transmission and distribution. The relative share of consumption in the different consumption bands is reported by the countries and used to calculated the single national natural gas prices (weighted averages for consumer bands IA-IF and DA-DE).

passages.title: Gas prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_202)
passages.text:
Some of the taxes are refundable, as defined in the national metadata.

Since reference period 2021 semester 2, countries report subsidies and allowances to alleviate the increased energy costs. Detailed description is available in the national metadata.

passages.title: Trade by partner country (nrg_t)
passages.text:
Annual imports and exports data of various energy carriers, such as crude oil and petroleum products, natural gas, electricity, solid fossil fuels and combustible renewables by country of origin and destination.

Annual data collection cover in principle the EU Member States, EFTA, EU candidate countries, and potential candidate countries. Time series starts mostly in year 1990.

For solid fossil fuels, natural gas, crude oil, oil products and biofuels the partner country of the "imports” refer to the country of ultimate origin, the country in which the energy product was produced. Partner country of the "exports” refer to the ultimate country of consumption of the energy products.

passages.title: Trade by partner country (nrg_t)
passages.text: For electricity the partner country of the "imports” refer to the country from where the electricity enters, the partner country of the "exports” is the country where the electricity exits on the borders. If electricity is transited through a country, the amount should be reported as both an import and an export.

passages.title: Solar thermal collectors' surface (nrg_inf_stcs)
passages.text: Energy domain provides highly comparable annual energy statistics. Eurostat verifies, to the extent possible, if the reported data respect the prescribed methodology. Occasional breaks in time series are present due to the developments of statistical systems on national level and the level of detailed information (micro data) available at national level.

In general comparability is very high in last 10 years and for older periods slowly decreasing. In addition, introduction of new statistical information in the most recent data collections can lead to breaks in series until information is compiled and provided by reporting countries.

passages.title: Electricity prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_204)
passages.text: Household sector and final non-household sector (industry, services, offices, agriculture, etc).

passages.title: Electricity prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_204)
passages.text:
The prices are reported in national currencies per kWh and according to different bands of consumption.

For the household sector, these bands are:

- DA: customers consuming less than 1000 kWh.

- DB: customers consuming 1000 kWh or more but less than 2500 kWh.

- DC: customers consuming 2500 kWh or more but less than 5000 kWh.

- DD: customers consuming 5000 kWh or more but less than 15000 kWh.

- DE: customers consuming 15000 kWh or more.

For the final non-household sector, the bands are:

- IA: customers consuming less than 20 MWh.

- IB: customers consuming 20 MWh or more but less than 500 MWh.

- IC: customers consuming 500 MWh or more but less than 2000 MWh.

passages.title: Electricity prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_204)
passages.text:
- ID: customers consuming 2000 MWh or more but less than 20000 MWh.

- IE: customers consuming 20000 MWh or more but less than 70000 MWh.

- IF: customers consuming 70000 MWh or more but less than 150000 MWh.

- IG: customers consuming 150000 MWh or more.

There exist 2 different levels of disagregation for semestrial and annual prices:

1- Semestrial prices:

These prices are reported twice a year and are divided in 3 levels:

- Level 1 prices: prices excluding taxes and levies.

- Level 2 prices: prices excluding VAT and other recoverable taxes and levies.

- Level 3 prices: prices including all taxes and levies.

2- Annual prices:

passages.title: Electricity prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_204)
passages.text:
These prices are reported once a year together with the data for the second semester and are divided into the following components and taxes:

- Energy and supply: generation, aggregation, balancing energy, supplied energy costs, customer services, after-sales management and other supply costs.

- Network cost: transmission and distribution tariffs, transmission and distribution losses, network costs, after-sale service costs, system service costs, and meter rental and metering costs.

- Value added taxes (VAT): as defined in Council Directive 2006/112/EC.

passages.title: Electricity prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_204)
passages.text:
- Renewable taxes: taxes, fees, levies or charges relating to the promotion of renewable energy sources, energy efficiency and CHP generation.

- Capacity taxes: Taxes, fees, levies or charges relating to capacity payments, energy security and generation adequacy; taxes on coal industry restructuring; taxes on electricity distribution; stranded costs and levies on financing energy regulatory authorities or market and system operators.

- Environmental taxes: taxes, fees, levies or charges relating to air quality and for other environmental purposes; taxes on emissions of CO 2  or other greenhouse gases. This component includes the excise duties.

passages.title: Electricity prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_204)
passages.text:
- Nuclear taxes: taxes, fees, levies or charges relating to the nuclear sector, including nuclear decommissioning, inspections and fees for nuclear installations.

- All other taxes: taxes, fees, levies or charges not covered by any of the previous five categories: support for district heating; local or regional fiscal charges; island compensation; concession fees relating to licences and fees for the occupation of land and public or private property by networks or other devices.

passages.title: Electricity prices - bi-annual data (from 2007 onwards) (nrg_pc_204)
passages.text:
In addition to these elements, the network cost is split into the respective shares of transmission and distribution. The relative share of consumption in the different consumption bands is reported by the countries and used to calculated the single national electricity prices (weighted averages for consumer bands IA-IG and DA-DE).

Some of the taxes are refundable, as defined in the national metadata.

Since reference period 2021 semester 2, countries report subsidies and allowances to alleviate the increased energy costs. Detailed description is available in the national metadata.

passages.title: Energy statistics - cooling and heating degree days (nrg_chdd)
passages.text:
Heating degree day (HDD) index is a weather-based technical index designed to describe the need for the heating energy requirements of buildings. Cooling degree day (CDD) index is a weather-based technical index designed to describe the need for the cooling (air-conditioning) requirements of buildings.

HDD and CDD are derived from meteorological observations of air temperature, interpolated to regular grids at 25 km resolution for Europe. Calculated gridded HDD and CDD are aggregated and subsequently presented on NUTS-3 level.

passages.title: Energy statistics - cooling and heating degree days (nrg_chdd)
passages.text: This dataset includes monthly data as published by the Joint Research Centre's AGRI4CAST Resources Portal (Note that Eurostat is not the producer of the monthly data, but is only re-publishing them). Annual data are calculated as sum of monthly data by Eurostat.

passages.title: Energy statistics - cooling and heating degree days (nrg_chdd)
passages.text:
NUTS-3 regions as adopted by Commission Regulation (EC) No 105/2007 (also known as NUTS 2006 applicable in period 2008-2011).

Further updates of NUTS classification by Commission Regulation (EU) No 31/2011 ,  Commission Regulation (EU) No 1319/2013 ,   Commission Regulation (EU) No 868/2014 and  Commission Regulation (EU) 2016/2066 are not implemented in this dataset.

passages.title: Energy statistics - cooling and heating degree days (nrg_chdd)
passages.text: Heating Degree Days (HDD) index:   the severity of the cold in a specific time period taking into consideration outdoor temperature and average room temperature (in other words the need for heating). The calculation of HDD relies on the base temperature, defined as the lowest daily mean air temperature not leading to indoor heating. The value of the base temperature depends in principle on several factors associated with the building and the surrounding environment. By using a general climatological approach, the base temperature is set to a constant value of 15°C in the HDD calculation.

passages.title: Energy statistics - cooling and heating degree days (nrg_chdd)
passages.text:
If T m ≤ 15°C Then [HDD = ∑ i ( 18°C - T i m )] Else [HDD = 0]  where T i m  is the mean air temperature of day i.

Examples: If the daily mean air temperature is 12°C, for that day the value of the HDD index is 6 (18°C-12°C). If the daily mean air temperature is 16°C, for that day the HDD index is 0.

passages.title: Energy statistics - cooling and heating degree days (nrg_chdd)
passages.text: Cooling degree days (CDD) index:   the severity of the heat in a specific time period taking into consideration outdoor temperature and average room temperature (in other words the need for cooling). The calculation of CDD relies on the base temperature, defined as the highest daily mean air temperature not leading to indoor cooling. The value of the base temperature depends in principle on several factors associated with the building and the surrounding environment. By using a general climatological approach, the base temperature is set to a constant value of 24°C in the CDD calculation.

passages.title: Energy statistics - cooling and heating degree days (nrg_chdd)
passages.text:
If T m ≥ 24°C Then [CDD = ∑ i T i m  - 2 1°C) ] Else [CDD = 0]   where T i m  is the mean air temperature of day i.

Examples: If the daily mean air temperature is 26°C, for that day the value of the CDD index is 5 (26°C-21°C). If the daily mean air temperature is 22°C, for that day the CDD index is 0.



These calculations are executed on a daily basis, added up to a calendar months and subsequently to  calendar years.

passages.text: Gridded meteorological data from temperature measuring stations.

passages.text: The HDD and CDD estimates for the EU are based on observations from about 3000 weather stations across Europe.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.text:
Statistics on the production and consumption of coal.

Data extracted in May and July 2026

Planned article update: August 2027

In 2025, the EU production of hard coal was 44 million tonnes, 84% less than the 277 million tonnes of 1990.
From 2018 to 2025, the EU halved its consumption of both hard coal (52%) and brown coal (50%).
In 2024, solar overtook coal as a source of electricity for the first time in the EU.
In 2024, the EU’s hard coal import dependency rate decreased to 57.2%, its lowest level since 2007.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.text:
This article explains how consumption and supply of coal in the European Union (EU), the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) and in candidate and potential candidate countries (with a specific focus on Western Balkan countries) have evolved, highlighting the trends in production and consumption of the main types of solid fossil fuels: hard coal and brown coal.

In addition, the article gives some figures on the supply of coke oven coke.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Consumption and production of hard coal
passages.text: As illustrated in Figure 1, inland consumption of hard coal in the EU decreased steadily in the 1990s. Starting in 1999 and for almost a decade, the yearly hard coal consumption stabilised at around 300 million tonnes. After a first sharp decline in 2008 and another in 2009, consumption stabilised around a new plateau of 250 million tonnes from 2010 onwards. In 2019, another strong decline started, amplified by the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. The 2025 hard coal consumption of the EU is estimated to have reached 107 million tonnes, 52% less than 8 years ago.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Consumption and production of hard coal
passages.text: Production of hard coal in the EU has decreased almost continuously from 1990, more consistently than consumption. In 2024, EU production was 44 million tonnes, 84% less than the 277 million tonnes of 1990. In 2025, 41% of inland consumption could be covered by production in the EU, compared with 71% in 1990. The gap between the 2 was mostly covered by imports (see Import dependency of hard coal). The 2025 figures are based on preliminary annual data.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Consumption and production of hard coal
passages.text: In 1990, 13 EU countries of the current EU were producing hard coal. In 2025, after the phaseout of hard coal production by Bulgaria in 2014, Italy in 2016, and Spain and Germany in 2019, there were only 2 hard coal producers left in the EU: Poland and Czechia. Poland produced 44 million tonnes of hard coal (97% of the total EU production) and Czechia produced 1.3 million tonnes (3%). Compared to 2012, which was the last peak in the EU hard coal production (106 million tonnes), in 2025 Poland decreased its production by 46% and Czechia by 89%.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Consumption and production of hard coal
passages.text: In 2025, Poland (45%) and Germany (23%) together accounted for two thirds of the total hard coal consumption in the EU, followed by the Netherlands, France, Belgium and Italy (each between 3% and 7%). Figure 2 presents the hard coal consumption in the EU countries from 2020 to 2025. With the exception of Malta, which stopped using hard coal in 1996, every other country in the EU reported consumption of hard coal ranging from a few thousand tonnes to several million tonnes.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Consumption and production of hard coal
passages.text:
One EFTA country, Norway, still produced hard coal in 2025. While stable in the 1990s at around 300 000 tonnes, Norway's hard coal production reached a peak of 4 million tonnes in 2007, before decreasing again to 93 000 tonnes in 2025, the year during which, in August, production stopped completely.

Consumption of hard coal by EFTA countries remained stable at around 1 million tonnes since 1990. In 2024, 2 EFTA countries, Norway and Iceland, reported a hard coal consumption of 840 000 tonnes.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Consumption and production of hard coal
passages.text: In 2025, 2 candidate countries produced hard coal: Türkiye and Albania. Production in Türkiye hovered between 2 and 3 million tonnes from 1990 to 2013, but then decreased, reaching a new plateau of around 1.3 million tonnes in the mid-2010s. Albania started producing hard coal in small quantities in 2015; in 2025, the production reached 236 000 tonnes.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Consumption and production of hard coal
passages.text: With the exception of Montenegro, every candidate and potential candidate country reported a consumption of hard coal ranging from a few thousand tonnes to several million tonnes. Consumption of hard coal in the Western Balkans never exceeded 3 million tonnes; in 2025, it reached just below 1 million tonnes, with Bosnia and Herzegovina representing half of the region's consumption.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.text: Solid fossil fuels had a lower energy dependency rate of 34.2% in 2024 compared with other fossil fuels, such as oil or natural gas (see Statistics Explained article on Energy statistics - an overview). However, this dependency rate accounts for all solid fossil fuels, including brown coal (with a high production and negligible trade) and many secondary products where the EU is a net exporter. Hard coal is the main type of coal with a noticeable import dependency, reaching 57.2% in 2024.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.text: The curves for both solid fossil fuels and hard coal import dependency followed similar patterns (see Figure 3). Starting in 1990 at 18.7% for solid fossil fuels and 29.6% for hard coal, import dependency began to increase in the middle of the 1990s. By 2004, the rate of increase was slowing down, before reaching a temporary high point in 2018. After decreasing in 2020 and 2021, import dependency increased in 2022 to reach its highest level for both curves, with a rate of 45.9% for solid fossil fuels and 74.5% for hard coal. Another strong decrease in dependency rate started shortly after, and in 2024, import dependency reached its lowest level since 2007 for hard coal and since 2003 for solid fossil fuels.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.text: The long-term increase in import dependency is due to the decrease in production observed since 1990 outpacing the one in consumption, with the gap between the 2 mostly filled by imports. In contrast, the peaks reached in 2022 could be partly explained by the consequences of the Russian war of aggression against Ukraine. In the 2010s, imports from most of the traditionally important hard coal suppliers decreased or remained stable while consumption of hard coal in the EU decreased. The exception was Russia, for which EU countries reported an increase in imports reaching a high of 61 million tonnes in 2018. 4%) of the EU's hard coal imports.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.text:
However, on 8 April 2022, the EU agreed on a ban of imports of coal from Russia in its fifth package of sanctions, with the ban entering into force in August 2022. 5% compared to 2021. 6%) (see Figure 4).

Coal imports also depend on market prices and other factors, which can lead to changes in suppliers. Traditional hard coal suppliers to the EU such as Ukraine, Venezuela or Norway have seen their imports decrease in recent years; at the same time, new suppliers such as Kazakhstan, Mozambique, Tanzania or Peru have emerged.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Consumption and production of brown coal
passages.text: The 2025 consumption of brown coal in the EU is estimated at 184 million tonnes, 50% less than in 2018. Figure 5 presents the trend since 1990. In the 1990s, the consumption decreased rapidly, broadly stagnating between 2000 and 2015 in a range of 400 to 450 million tonnes per year. From 2018 to 2020, consumption decreased sharply, before increasing again in 2021 and 2022. With another large decrease from 2023 onwards, the EU consumption of brown coal is now estimated at a historical low.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Consumption and production of brown coal
passages.text:
The brown coal production trend is very similar to its consumption trend; brown coal is mostly consumed in the countries where it is produced, while imports and exports are negligible. The 2025 figures are based on preliminary annual data.

In 1990, 15 EU countries of the current EU were producing brown coal. This number slowly decreased over the following decades. Spain stopped its production in 2019, and Slovakia in 2024. Today, 8 EU countries still produce and consume brown coal in the EU.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Consumption and production of brown coal
passages.text:
In 2025, Germany represented 46% of the total brown coal consumption in the EU, followed by Poland (21%), Czechia (13%), Bulgaria (10%), Romania (7%) and Greece (3%). Figure 6 presents the brown coal consumption in the EU countries from 2019 to 2025.

Brown coal is absent from the EFTA countries' energy mix (production and consumption).

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Consumption and production of brown coal
passages.text: Unlike in the EU, brown coal consumption increased in candidate countries. It reached 147 million tonnes in 2025, 35% higher than in 1990. Türkiye accounted for 60% of this total consumption, having almost doubled its consumption from 46 million tonnes in 1990 to 88 million tonnes in 2025. The Western Balkan countries accounted for most of the remaining 40%, with Georgia and Moldova reporting minor consumptions of 168 000 tonnes and 900 tonnes respectively.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Consumption and production of brown coal
passages.text: In 1990, 3 countries were producing and consuming brown coal in the Western Balkans: Albania, North Macedonia and Serbia. Their combined consumption reached 54 million tonnes. From the year 2000, the 3 other Western Balkan countries also started producing brown coal. Western Balkan countries consumed 58 million tonnes of brown coal in 2025, an increase of 7% compared with 1990. The largest brown coal producer and consumer in the Western Balkans was Serbia, accounting for 60% of brown coal consumption in the region. In Albania, Montenegro, North Macedonia and Kosovo*, the production and consumption never exceeded 10 million tonnes per year. Albania stopped its production in 2013, but started it again in 2023 in very low quantities, with almost all of them being exported.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Consumption and production of brown coal
passages.text: Kosovo*: This designation is without prejudice to positions on status and is in line with UNSCR 1244/99 and the ICJ Opinion on the Kosovo Declaration of Independence.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Deliveries of coal to power plants
passages.text:
In the EU, almost half of the quantities of hard coal (45% in 2024) and a large majority of brown coal (92% in 2024) is used for power production. In 2024, 50 million tonnes of hard coal were delivered to power plants producing electricity and heat in the EU. For brown coal, this amount was 185 million tonnes. The 2025 figures are based on preliminary annual data.

Figure 7 shows that from 2013 to 2020, both hard coal and brown coal deliveries for power production showed declining trends, which accelerated in 2019 and 2020. After increases in deliveries in 2021 and 2022, they strongly fell in 2023 and 2024 to reach their lowest levels on record.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Deliveries of coal to power plants
passages.text: In the EFTA countries, deliveries of hard coal to power plants fluctuated around 30 000 tonnes between 1990 and 2023, and stopped completely in 2024; they represented only a marginal use of hard coal (3% in 2023) as EFTA countries use hard coal mainly in their industry sector. In candidate and potential candidate countries, deliveries of hard coal to power plants, mainly by Türkiye, reached 28 million tonnes in 2024, representing 65% of the use of hard coal. As in the EU, a large majority of brown coal used in candidate countries was delivered to power plants: 129 million tonnes, or 91% of brown coal consumption. An even higher percentage of 98% was observed in Western Balkan countries.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Deliveries of coal to power plants
passages.text: Brown coal has a low energy content, and does not have a lot of potential uses besides electricity and heat generation. In most EU countries using brown coal in 2024, at least 90% of brown coal was used to produce electricity and heat (see Figure 8). In Hungary, Poland, Greece, Slovenia, as well as Montenegro, Serbia, North Macedonia and Kosovo, this share reached more than 98%. In countries where the shares were lower, such as Slovakia, Bulgaria, Germany or Türkiye, brown coal was also used to produce other energy products such as brown coal briquettes, for industry purposes, and sometimes by households to heat their homes.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Deliveries of coal to power plants
passages.text: Contrary to brown coal, hard coal has a wide variety of applications in the industry sector, for example in coke ovens (see Figure 12). Hard coal has a high energy content and thus can produce electricity and heat more effectively than brown coal. However, because of its environmental and health issues, countries replace it more and more with natural gas and renewable energy sources.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Deliveries of coal to power plants
passages.text: Since 1990, the importance of coal in electricity production decreased almost continuously, with slight rebounds in 2011 and 2021-2022 (see Figure 9). In 1990, coal (hard coal and brown coal) was the largest source of electricity in the EU, with a share of 35% of electricity generation. This share was overtaken by nuclear heat in 1994, by natural gas in 2019, by hydro and wind in 2023 and by solar in 2024.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Deliveries of coal to power plants
passages.text: In 1990, hard coal and brown coal were respectively the second and third largest source of electricity production in the EU, with respectively 20% and 15% of the gross production. In contrast in 2025, 4% of total gross electricity produced in the EU was based on hard coal and 5% on brown coal, representing respectively around 106 000 GWh and 154 000 GWh (see Figure 9): they were respectively the seventh and sixth source of electricity generation, behind nuclear heat, natural gas and renewable fuels.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Deliveries of coal to power plants
passages.text: In candidate and potential candidate countries, coal played a much more important role in electricity generation. In these countries, the shares of hard coal and brown coal used in the production of electricity reached 17% and 19% respectively in 2024, comparable to natural gas (16%), but lower than hydro (25%). This large share for coal was particularly striking in Western Balkan countries, where brown coal was the single largest source of electricity production; with around 43 000 GWh of production in 2024, brown coal provided 55% of the electricity consumed in the Western Balkans, ahead of hydro with 33% (see Figure 10). Despite the critical importance of brown coal in the Western Balkans’ energy mix, its share has declined to the benefit of renewables in recent years.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Deliveries of coal to power plants
passages.text: In 2024, 19 EU countries used hard coal in their production of electricity; however, this share of hard coal went above 0.5% in only 12 of these countries. The only EU country where hard coal played a significant role in electricity generation was Poland; with a share of 33%, hard coal was the first source of electricity. In other EU countries, the share of hard coal did not exceed 7% of electricity production. In candidate countries, hard coal only played a major role in the production of electricity in Türkiye, with a share of 22%, compared to 12% for brown coal.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Deliveries of coal to power plants
passages.text: In 2024, brown coal was used in electricity generation in the 9 EU countries that were producing it, as well as in 5 Western Balkan countries and Türkiye. In contrast to hard coal, brown coal is sometimes a major source of electricity production. However, whereas in recent years brown coal supplied more than 40% of electricity in many EU countries, in 2023 its shares declined dramatically. In 2024, its share in electricity generation reached 34% in Czechia, and 21% in Bulgaria, Poland and Slovenia. In contrast, brown coal still played a major role in electricity generation in Western Balkan countries, providing 37% of the electricity generation in North Macedonia, 40% in Montenegro, 61% in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 63% in Serbia and 91% in Kosovo (see Figure 11).

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Deliveries of coal to power plants
passages.text: When adding both types of coal together, Poland stood out as the only EU country in which coal was the largest source of electricity, and the only one in which more than half of electricity generation relied on coal (55%). Coal was the second-largest source of electricity in Czechia (36%) and Bulgaria (21%) behind nuclear heat, and in Germany (21%) behind wind. Finally, coal was the third-largest source of electricity in Slovenia (21%) behind nuclear heat and hydro. In non-EU countries, coal was the largest source of electricity in Kosovo (91%), Serbia (63%), Bosnia and Herzegovina (61%), North Macedonia (37%) and Türkiye (34%); it was the second-largest source of electricity in Montenegro (40%) behind hydro.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Deliveries of coal to power plants
passages.text: In much smaller quantities, hard coal and brown coal still play a role in the production of heat. In 2025, 11% of total gross heat produced in the EU was based on hard coal (around 224 000 TJ) and 3% on brown coal (around 69 000 TJ); compared with 1990, their respective shares decreased by 24% and 13%. In 1990, hard coal was the first source of heat production in the EU, but it has been progressively replaced by natural gas and primary solid biofuels.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.section: Deliveries of coal to coking plants and coke oven coke production
passages.text:
Hard coal (more specifically coking coal) is essential to produce coke oven coke for the steel and iron industry. In 2024, coke ovens in 12 EU countries consumed 36 million tonnes of coking coal to produce 27 million tonnes of coke oven coke. Coke oven activity was stable until 2018, after which it started to decline, reaching a new plateau from 2020 onwards, before declining again in 2023 and 2024 (see Figure 12).

No activity for coke ovens was recorded in EFTA countries. In candidate and potential candidate countries, 2 countries reported an activity for coke ovens in 2024, using 6 million tonnes of coking coal to produce 5 million tonnes of coke oven coke.

passages.title: Coal production and consumption statistics
passages.text: The reporting of coal statistics is based on Energy statistics Regulation (EC) No 1099/2008 on energy statistics. The production and consumption data of hard coal, brown coal and coke oven coke between 1990 and 2024 are based on annual statistics (Annex B of the Regulation). The data related to electricity production and the share of coal in it are based on data from the annual electricity and heat questionnaire. For the latest available 2025 data, preliminary annual data was used.
